subject: physics

unit.name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
question_text: Find the centre of mass of three particles at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. The masses of the particles are 100 g, 150 g and 200 g respectively. Each side of the equilateral triangle is 0.5 m long.

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 7 SHORT ANSWER 8 — printed exam years "(2004, 05, 10, 11)", recorded as TS appearances (claims until a teacher confirms; the pre-2014 papers are united-AP-era). The split is invented. Arithmetic hand-checked: x = 125/450 = 5/18 m; y = 86.6/450 = 1/(3√3) m.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Choose the axes
lines: Put the 100 g mass at the origin O and
the 150 g mass on the x-axis. Then:
steps.margin_note: B sits above the midpoint of OA at height (√3/2)·side. Write all three coordinate pairs before any formula.
steps.why: A good axis choice puts two masses on one axis — two zeros in the sums that follow. The physics is the same for any axes; the arithmetic is not.
common_mistakes: Taking B at (0.25, 0.5) — the height of an equilateral triangle is (√3/2)·side, not the side.

recall.must_convey: That the three vertices get coordinates with 100 g at the origin and B at (0.25, 0.25√3).
accept: put hundred grams at the origin
B is at point two five comma point two five root three
reject: x of centre of mass is five by eighteen

steps.label: The triangle
steps.margin_note: Drawn to scale, the CM cross sits visibly nearer the 200 g vertex — a built-in sanity check on the answer.
steps.why: The centre of mass must lean towards the heaviest particle. If the computed point lands elsewhere, the arithmetic is wrong.
common_mistakes: Placing the CM at the centroid. The centroid is for EQUAL masses only.

recall.must_convey: That the triangle is drawn with the three masses and the centre of mass marked.
accept: draw the triangle with the masses
reject: put hundred grams at the origin

steps.label: x of the CM
steps.margin_note: One substitution line with all three products visible, then the fraction. Grams cancel — no unit conversion needed.
steps.why: Grams appear in every term of the numerator and the denominator, so they cancel; converting to kg first is honest work for nothing.
common_mistakes: Converting each mass to kg and losing a factor of 1000 in one term.

recall.must_convey: That x of the centre of mass is the mass-weighted average, giving 5/18 m.

steps.label: y of the CM and the result
lines: The point lies towards the 200 g mass,
steps.margin_note: Close with the sanity line — "towards the heaviest mass". It costs nothing and shows understanding.
steps.why: Only B has a y-coordinate, so the y-sum has one term. The final check against the figure is the habit that catches sign and height errors.

recall.must_convey: That y of the centre of mass is 1/(3√3) m and the CM is (5/18, 1/(3√3)).
accept: y c m has only the B term
towards the two hundred gram mass
